newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin raps U.S. "hegemony" bid at G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Jospin raps U.S. "hegemony" bid at G7 summit.

text.p: Socialist French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin accused the United States on Tuesday of seeking to impose its economic and social model on Europe at last weekend's Group of Seven summit in Denver.

"I am not satisfied with the results of Denver ,"Jospin told parliament. "We see a certain tendency towards hegemony, which is not necessarily identical with exercising the global responsibilities of a great power, even if it is a friend."

The prime minister, who took office three weeks ago at the head of a coalition of Socialists, Communists and ecologists, did not attend the summit, at which conservative President Jacques Chirac represented France.
But Chirac was even more withering than Jospin in private comments made at the G7, according to the well-informed French weekly Le Canard Enchaine.
"We're wasting our time here," Chirac was quoted as saying in the unsourced report. "We're nothing but extras in Clinton's marketing plan".

The Americans "have already decided to do everything without us. They see us as crap," Chirac added, according to the weekly. Since Jospin's leftist government took power in a June 1 parliamentary election, "they take us for retarded."
In his remarks to parliament, Jospin said Europe did not have the same social model as the United States and had always tried to balance economic and social priorities.
"Europe does not have the United States' attributes of power and the rules that may apply in the wake of that considerable power...cannot be as effective in Europe," he said.

"It will be up to Europe's determination, and to France's own ability -- and my government will work to that end -- to ensure that Europe's concerns carry greater weight next time perhaps," Jospin added.

His criticism of President Bill Clinton's conduct of the summit, echoing overwhelmingly negative French media coverage, was made in response to a pre-arranged question from his own Socialist group at his first parliamentary question time.

French media accused Clinton on Monday of cowboy arrogance in lecturing Europe on jobs and growth when the United States had greater inequality, worse poverty, poorer social services and more violent crime than west European societies.
Jospin's comments reflected a bipartisan consensus that France should resist U.S. world dominance and defend its welfare state and mixed economy against the "Anglo-Saxon" model.
The G7 summit urged Europe's three biggest economies -- Germany, France and Italy -- to carry out structural reforms to combat their high unemployment.

In Denver, Chirac rejected calls to adopt wholesale American concepts of economic deregulation and welfare reduction to solve Europe's problem of high unemployment and slow growth, saying he remained attached to the European social model.

He also voiced irritation at Clinton's attempt to dictate that only three central European candidates -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- would be asked to join NATO at a summit of the 16-nation alliance in Madrid next month, even though most European allies favoured admitting Romania and Slovenia as well.

The disagreements set the stage for a possible clash at the July 8-9 summit, since the United States has also refused to accommodate French demands that it hand over NATO's key southern command, controlling the Mediterranean, to a European officer.

Jospin did not criticise the president's performance in Denver. He said he had not attended the summit himself because he was not interested in "formal representative roles", and that Socialist finance and foreign ministers had accompanied the president "because we did not want him to be alone".
Discussing his own role, Jospin said: "I will not go where my presence is not formally required, but I will go where the policy of the French government has to be put into effect."
